_comment: Hand-authored. The pairing is the editorial part of this page: which two commands count as
'the same job' is a judgement, and the page prints each tool's own description beside the
other so a reader can check it. Names in cc[] and cx[] are resolved by build.py against
claude-code-cheatsheet/commands.json and codex-cheatsheet/codex-commands.json — a name that
no longer exists fails the build rather than publishing a dead pairing. Everything not named
here lands in 'only in one of them', which is therefore a computed complement, not a list.

shape.cc: Almost everything is a slash command, and the shell side is a short list of things you do to Claude Code rather than with it — install it, log in, manage plugins.
shape.cx: The shell side is the bigger half, and it goes deep: codex app-server daemon enable-remote-control is a real command. Codex expects to be scripted and embedded, not only typed at.

pairs.note: Word for word the same sentence in both builds — the only entry on this page where the two descriptions are identical.
Codex splits it in two: /new starts the chat over, /clear also wipes the terminal. Claude Code keeps the old session on disk either way.
Same summarise-and-continue move. Claude Code additionally lets you set the trigger threshold and draw the context as a grid; Codex reports usage through /status.
Both offer a picker. Codex can also do it from the shell before launch, and takes --last to skip the picker.
Different word, same idea — keep this history, continue down a second path. Claude Code's /fork is not this; it spawns a background agent.
Codex's /side answers to the alias btw — the same name Claude Code gives the command, which it keeps out of /help.
Claude Code takes an index — /copy 3 for the third-latest.
Codex folds token usage into the same command; Claude Code puts that in /context and /usage.
Codex has no separate command — its own /model description says it picks “what model and reasoning effort to use”. Claude Code splits the two.
Same name, and both are explicit that you are not being downgraded to a smaller model — you are paying for speed.

pairs.job: Set a goal to hold to
pairs.note: Claude Code checks it before stopping; Codex frames it as the goal for a long-running task.
The one place the two ecosystems visibly diverge: CLAUDE.md against AGENTS.md. Same command, different filename.
Codex includes untracked files; Claude Code adds a per-turn view of what it changed.

pairs.job: Review the changes you have not committed
pairs.note: Codex exposes review three ways, one of them non-interactive and scriptable. Claude Code's is a bundled skill, and it ships a second one that applies cleanups rather than reporting them.
Claude Code can move mid-session; Codex settles it at launch. The flag spellings are identical.

pairs.job: Decide what it may do without asking
pairs.note: Same command name, different model underneath — see the capability table below.
Claude Code toggles a sandbox for its own Bash tool. Codex also ships the sandbox as a shell command you can wrap any process in, agent or not.

pairs.job: Run your own code on lifecycle events

pairs.note: Claude Code has a settings UI and a skill that rewrites the file for you. Codex expects you to edit config.toml; its config command is hidden and read-only — it shows which layer a value came from.
Codex will also put session items in the terminal's title bar.
Codex ships a Vim mode for the composer; Claude Code ships a skill that edits the keybindings file with you.
Both keep memory outside the conversation and let you pause or shape it.
Both ship it, and Codex names its source out loud: “import setup, this project, and recent chats from Claude Code.”
Claude Code manages an integration; Codex pulls your selection and open files in as context.
Claude Code additionally reloads them mid-session and reports which loaded skills are costing you context for nothing.
Codex breaks the shell side into one subcommand per operation, including login and logout for servers behind auth.
Both have marketplaces. Codex's are explicit config entries you add, list, upgrade and remove by name.
Codex has no /login at the prompt — signing in is a shell command.
Claude Code adds a plain-words breakdown of where a session's tokens went and a report across sessions.
Both check installation, config and auth. Claude Code's also runs inside a session.
Claude Code can swap the binary without dropping the conversation.
The scripting entry point on both. Claude Code drives it with flags — --output-format, --json-schema, --max-budget-usd; Codex gives exec its own subcommands.
The names line up and the meanings do not. Claude Code backgrounds whole sessions and agents; Codex's /ps and /stop list and kill the shell processes the agent started.

Codex switches which agent thread you are typing at. Claude Code sends work away and brings the result back, and its /agents entry says the command was removed in favour of editing .claude/agents/ directly.
Claude Code hands off to a phone or claude.ai; Codex pairs a daemon you connect a front-end to.
Both send work off-machine and bring a diff back. Codex's is a general task queue you drive from the shell; Claude Code's is job-shaped — review this branch, draft this plan.

capabilities.cc: ~/.claude/settings.json — JSON, with a /config UI and a bundled skill that rewrites it for you.
capabilities.cx: ~/.codex/config.toml — TOML, layered. Any key is overridable per-run with -c foo.bar=value, and --profile <name> stacks $CODEX_HOME/<name>.config.toml on top.
capabilities.evidence: Both files on this machine, plus codex --help.

capabilities.cc: CLAUDE.md, written by /init, auto-discovered up the tree.
capabilities.evidence: Each tool's own /init description, and both files present in the two config homes.

capabilities.cc: One axis. --permission-mode takes acceptEdits, auto, bypassPermissions, manual, dontAsk or plan, with allow/deny rules per tool underneath.
capabilities.cx: Two orthogonal axes. --ask-for-approval takes untrusted, on-request or never; --sandbox independently takes read-only, workspace-write or danger-full-access.
capabilities.evidence: The [possible values] block each CLI prints for those flags in --help.

capabilities.cc: /sandbox toggles sandboxing for the Bash tool, on supported platforms only. It applies to what Claude Code runs.
capabilities.cx: The same sandbox is also a command you can point at anything: codex sandbox -- <cmd> runs it under seatbelt, and --log-denials prints the macOS denials it collected.
capabilities.evidence: codex sandbox --help; the /sandbox description in the build.

capabilities.cc: --dangerously-skip-permissions, plus --allow-dangerously-skip-permissions to make it available without turning it on.
capabilities.cx: --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox, and separately --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust for running hooks whose source has not been vetted.

capabilities.cc: Configured under hooks in settings.json. The binary carries eleven event names: PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PermissionRequest, UserPromptSubmit, Notification, PreCompact, SessionStart, SessionEnd, Stop, SubagentStart, SubagentStop.
capabilities.cx: A separate ~/.codex/hooks.json, with per-hook trust recorded back into config.toml under hooks.state — Codex will not run a hook it has not been trusted to run.
capabilities.evidence: Event names read out of the Claude Code binary; the Codex side read off the two config files. See the caveat below the table.

capabilities.cc: 35 compiled into the binary — the whole prompt corpus is on its own page here — plus whatever is in ~/.claude/skills. 23 of the bundled ones are typeable as slash commands.
capabilities.cx: /skills, loading from ~/.codex/skills and from plugins. Whether Codex also bundles prompts of its own is not established here — no equivalent extractor was written for it, and a Rust binary does not give them up the way a Bun-compiled JavaScript bundle does. Read that as a gap in this page, not a finding about Codex.
capabilities.evidence: The skills extraction behind the bundled-skills page; both skills directories on this machine. The Codex half is deliberately a non-claim.

capabilities.cc: Definitions in .claude/agents/ or inline via --agents <json>. /subtask and /fork send work off and bring the result back; /workflows tracks multi-agent runs.
capabilities.cx: /agent and /subagents switch which agent thread you are typing at. SubagentStart and SubagentStop exist as hook points.
capabilities.evidence: Both command inventories; ~/.claude/agents/; the hook state keys in config.toml.

capabilities.cc: A client. claude mcp manages servers; --mcp-config loads them from a file or string and --strict-mcp-config ignores everything else.
capabilities.cx: A client and a server: codex mcp-server starts Codex itself as an MCP server over stdio, so another agent can call it as a tool.
capabilities.evidence: codex --help; the flag tables on both index pages.

capabilities.cc: claude -p plus flags: --output-format json|stream-json, --json-schema for structured output, --max-budget-usd, --input-format, --include-partial-messages.
capabilities.cx: codex exec with its own subcommands (resume, review), plus codex app-server — a protocol daemon that will emit its own JSON Schema and TypeScript bindings for you.
capabilities.evidence: Both flag tables and subcommand trees.

capabilities.cc: Anthropic, with /setup-bedrock and /setup-vertex for the cloud resellers, --fallback-model when the default is overloaded, and --betas for API-key users.
capabilities.cx: OpenAI, with --oss and --local-provider lmstudio|ollama for running against a local model instead.

capabilities.cc: None user-facing. Gating is internal: ten commands are in the binary but withheld from /help, and some skills register only when a check passes.
capabilities.cx: codex features list prints 100 switches with a maturity stage each, 40 of them on in this build, toggleable per-run with --enable/--disable or persisted with codex features enable.
capabilities.evidence: Both index pages; the feature table is codex features list verbatim.

capabilities.cc: At the prompt. 129 of 143 entries are typed after a / — 96 native, 23 bundled skills, 10 hidden — leaving 14 shell subcommands.
capabilities.cx: In the shell. 68 of 122 entries are codex subcommands, against 54 typed after a / — the only one of the two where the shell side is the bigger half.
capabilities.evidence: Counted from the two inventories. Hidden commands are counted as slash commands on both sides, because that is how they are typed.

cc: You want the session itself to be the workspace. Claude Code puts almost everything behind a /, including things Codex settles at launch — move to another directory, change effort, swap the model, background the whole session and get the terminal back.
You want to undo. /rewind has no counterpart on the Codex side of this page.
You lean on skills and subagents. 35 prompts ship in the binary, agents are files you write, and /subtask, /fork and /workflows exist to fan work out and collect it.
You want the model choice to include Bedrock or Vertex.
cx: You want the agent under a sandbox you can reason about — and reuse. Approval policy and sandbox policy are separate flags with named values, and codex sandbox will wrap any command, not just the agent's.
You are building on top of it. codex mcp-server makes Codex a tool other agents call; codex app-server hands you a protocol daemon with generated schema and TypeScript bindings.
You want the tool configured as data. One TOML file, layered profiles, and -c any.key=value for a single run.
You want to run against a local model — --oss with LM Studio or Ollama.
You want to see the feature flags rather than discover them.
verdict.both: Neither list is a ranking, and the overlap is the real story: 43 jobs on this page have a command on both sides, several with the same name. Both ship hooks, MCP, plugins, skills, plan mode, a review command, a memory system and a desktop hand-off. Both also ship a command that imports the other one's setup, which tells you what the vendors expect you to be doing.
